title: Synonymous, non-synonymous and premature stop snips

segs.text: Section four. snip types in coding regions. A single nucleotide polymorphism is one base pair changed in a gene. Several million are known, and many change nothing about the gene's product. Coding regions are the parts transcribed to R N A and then translated to protein. A codon is three bases coding one amino acid, and a coding snip is classed by what it does to the codon: same amino acid, synonymous; different amino acid, non-synonymous; early stop codon, premature stop.

Synonymous example: A B C B one, thirty four thirty five, C to T, the gene for P-glycoprotein. A T C becomes A T T, but several codons code the same amino acid, and both give isoleucine. She said, Synonymous means the same. It does not mean harmless: this snip keeps turning up in drug-response studies; she thinks expression is probably affected, but there is no consensus on function or expression. Affected drugs: efavirenz and cyclosporine.

Non-synonymous example: T P M T star three A. At six fifteen, G to A turns G C A, alanine, into A C A, threonine. At eight seventy four, A to G turns T A T, tyrosine, into T G T, cysteine. Each puts a different amino acid into the enzyme, so activity is significantly reduced. Azathioprine and six mercaptopurine depend on T P M T. She said, you could kill your patient if you didn't genotype them for this snip.

Premature stop example: sip two C nineteen star three. G to A turns T G G, tryptophan, into T A G, a stop codon, far earlier than the normal stop. The protein is truncated and activity is none, not low. A stop codon changes the protein, so a premature stop counts as non-synonymous. Affected drugs: the proton pump inhibitors omeprazole and lansoprazole.
